title: Digging Into the Subsoil: Considering and Theorizing Human Services Delivery at the Sub‐Micro‐Level of the Public Service Ecosystem
authors: Kate Broadhurst; Steven Parker
affiliations: Loughborough Business School Loughborough University Loughborough UK; Department for Public Leadership and Social Enterprise Open University Milton Keynes UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Public services are often delivered in partnership with families and communities, yet these relationships receive limited attention within public service ecosystem (PSE) theory. Responding to call to develop the sub‐micro‐level of the PSE, we introduce the concept of subsoil sensitivity to foreground the family and community ecosystems that underpin public service value creation. These informal systems are active sites of value creation and destruction with sensitivities arising from their alignment or misalignment with public services. We propose legislative and policy nodes as connectors that translate macrolevel policy into microlevel practice. Drawing on child protection vignettes, we show how nodes create the conditions for interaction, while subsoil dynamics influence whether value is cocreated or codestroyed amid power asymmetries and differing belief systems. The paper extends the sub‐micro‐level of the PSE and offers a framework for examining family and community ecosystems in public service delivery.

title: Political uncertainty, social legitimacy, and nonmarket strategy
authors: Jonathan Doh
abstract: Abstract The Decade Award–winning article by Darendeli and Hill (2016) presents a novel yet nuanced approach to the question of whether and how foreign firms can strategically navigate a volatile and unpredictable political environment. Their 2026 retrospective builds on their earlier contribution by showing how their insights have contributed to a number of contemporary IB research streams, including those addressing political risk, political action, and political ties. Going beyond their earlier contribution, in the retrospective, they describe the relational and physical pillars of social legitimacy (Darendeli & Hill, 2026). They then assess the efficacy of their original perspective in an environment characterized by heightened geopolitical conflict and political polarization. Finally, they develop a model that delineates four strategic approaches to legitimacy building in host countries. In this commentary, I offer perspectives that complement and extend their contributions by discussing (1) the nature of political uncertainty and the use of real options in responding to that uncertainty, (2) the literature on substantive versus symbolic CSR and how that might further extend some of their insights, and (3) research regarding when and how multinational enterprises provide public goods and services typically provided by government. I conclude by outlining how Darendeli and Hill’s (2016, 2026) insights have relevance for contemporary practice and policy.

title: Estimation of Excess Inhalation Non‐Cancer and Cancer Risk From Volatile Organic Compound Mixtures in New York City Nail Salons
authors: A. Michael Ierardi; Rachel L. Thompson; Samantha Fisher; Kimberly Anderson; Jean Grassman; Brian Pavilonis
affiliations: Department of Environmental, Occupational, and Geospatial Health Sciences City University of New York Graduate School of Public Health and Health Policy (CUNY SPH) New York New York USA; Center for Systems & Community Design CUNY SPH New York New York USA; Insight Exposure & Risk Sciences Group Boulder Colorado USA; Field Studies Branch, Respiratory Health Division National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health Morgantown West Virginia USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Nail salon workers are acutely and chronically exposed to mixtures of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), yet health risks in New York City (NYC) salons have not been systematically assessed. We performed an occupational risk assessment using integrated real‐time total VOC (TVOC) monitoring and chemical‐specific sampling of 11 VOCs across five NYC salons. Median and peak exposures and their 95th percentile (upper‐bound) values were used in non‐cancer and cancer risk models using deterministic and probabilistic approaches. Deterministic non‐cancer risk modeling indicated hazard indices (HIs) were generally below the benchmark value of 1, with exceedances observed only using upper‐bound exposures in the salon with the highest VOC concentrations. The probabilistic non‐cancer assessment showed a similar pattern, with some salons having non‐negligible probabilities of HI exceedance despite median HIs below 1. Deterministic and probabilistic benzene cancer risk assessments indicated exceedances of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) de minimis benchmark under multiple exposure scenarios. Although VOC concentrations were below occupational exposure limits (OELs), incorporating exposure variability and uncertainty identified elevated non‐cancer and cancer risks under certain scenarios. Previous research has linked nail salon work to adverse health effects, including respiratory symptoms and developmental and reproductive effects, suggesting that current OELs may not adequately protect this workforce. Our results highlight the need for improved exposure limits, chemical mixture risk assessment methods, and health protections for nail salon workers.

title: Geo‐Setting Risk Assessment in Eurasia: A Multidimensional Framework and Strategies
authors: Jing Zhang; Suocheng Dong; Jingwen Li; Zeqi Zhao
affiliations: Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research Chinese Academy of Sciences Beijing China; College of Resources and Environment University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Beijing China; School of International Business Shaanxi Normal University Xi'an Shaanxi China
abstract: ABSTRACT Amid intensifying geopolitical tensions and climate‐related pressures, geo‐setting risk has become increasingly multidimensional. This analysis of geo‐setting risk in 16 Eurasian countries from 2010 to 2023, using a composite framework integrating regional geopolitical, political, economic, social, and ecological indicators, revealed marked spatial and temporal heterogeneity. Ukraine, Armenia, the Russian Federation, Georgia, and Azerbaijan were identified as high‐comprehensive‐risk countries, whereas other countries displayed distinct vulnerabilities across specific dimensions in 2023. The findings suggest that Eurasian geo‐setting risk cannot be reduced to the Russia–Ukraine conflict alone but reflects the combined influence of conflict exposure, governance conditions, economic structure, social pressure, and ecological constraints. A two‐dimensional typology linking comprehensive risk to the dominant mechanisms is proposed to support comparative risk profiling and differentiated governance discussions.

title: Rethinking the Anatomy of Passion: A Biopsychosocial Configurational Perspective on Antecedents of Work and Entrepreneurial Passion
authors: Olivia Aronson; Marina Astakhova; Alexander Hamrick; Charles Murnieks; Henry Switz
affiliations: Robins School of Business University of Richmond Richmond Virginia USA; Bloch School of Management University of Missouri‐Kansas City Kansas City Missouri USA; University of Richmond Richmond Virginia USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite over two decades of passion research, our understanding of how passion is construed remains fragmented and dominated by additive approaches that treat antecedents as isolated predictors (both theoretically and empirically). Drawing on the biopsychosocial (BPS) framework, we challenge prior research by reconceptualizing passion as a configurational phenomenon emerging through interdependent BPS conditions which combine in complex ways to form equifinal pathways to passion. In doing so, we comparatively analyze configurations associated with harmonious and obsessive passion across the two most frequently studied domains in the management literature: work and entrepreneurship. To empirically examine this configurational perspective, we employ fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), which is well equipped to test the equifinal, compensatory, and interdependent nature of configural constructs. Using two time‐lagged samples of employees and entrepreneurs, we identify multiple distinct configurations that not only differentiate harmonious from obsessive passion but also distinguish passion across the work and entrepreneurial domains. Our results demonstrate that passion is largely domain‐contingent, such that work and entrepreneurial passion are each associated with mostly unique BPS configurations rather than universally operating antecedents. Our study advances passion research by shifting attention from isolated net effects toward a holistic view of passion as a system of interdependent BPS predictors.

title: EXPRESS: Securing Supply Chains: Subsidies, Insurance, and Hybrid Incentives under Costly Verification
authors: Mohammad Nikoofal; Manaf Zargoush; Saeed Beheshti; Mehmet Gümüş; Mahsa Madani-Hosseini
abstract: The rising frequency of supply-chain disruptions—driven by physical shocks and cyber intrusions—underscores the need for coordinated action between governments and private firms. Firms may underinvest in security because they do not internalize the broader social losses generated by supply-chain disruptions. Public intervention is complicated, however, because firms privately know their baseline network security, choose unobservable preventive effort, and are subject to costly and imperfect verification. We develop a game-theoretic framework to compare three policy approaches: an ex-ante, audit-based subsidy; an ex-post, inspection-based insurance mechanism; and hybrid mechanisms that combine preventive support with contingent protection. Insurance performs better in lower-security environments, where incidents under shirking remain sufficiently likely for claims inspection and denied coverage to provide credible deterrence. Subsidies perform better in moderate-to-high-security environments, where pre-incident verification remains effective even as disruptions become less frequent. In regions where both instruments are feasible, we use an efficiency index—prevention per unit of agency cost—to identify the preferred mechanism. We then analyze two hybrid designs. Under delayed inspection, the government provides an up-front subsidy but conditions coverage on post-incident verification. Under early audit, the government verifies compliance before activating both subsidy and coverage. These hybrids can outperform pure mechanisms when effective verification friction is high or when firms face a large investment-benefit gap. The results provide three policy implications. First, governments should segment firms by baseline network security rather than apply a uniform program. Second, improving verification accuracy can be as important as reducing its direct cost. Third, hybrid mechanisms are most appropriate when their stronger incentives justify the additional administrative and compliance burden of layered verification.

title: From a distance: How the social organisation of labour conditions personal attachment to work
authors: Anne Gravelle Antoni; Hamza Asshidi; Janna Rose; Nathalie Louisgrand
affiliations: Grenoble Ecole de Management, Grenoble, France; Université Grenoble Alpes, France
abstract: Employees are more often than not personally invested in their work. Such affective investment has been both praised as a potential source of self-fulfilment and condemned as a form of labour extraction. However, we aim to examine how employees in white-collar jobs navigate the multiple work and labour facets of their employment. Using the COVID-19 pandemic as a revelatory context, with the unexpected collapse of work-life articulations, we draw upon 50 semi-structured interviews of employees in a French private organisation of higher education. We show how individuals interrogated their investment in their employment as labour, yet not into their work as subjective endeavour. Moreover, we analyse how the material and social context of the social organisation of labour conditions individuals’ personal attachment to work. Finally, we discuss the struggle for a meaningful experience of working in higher education after decades of new public management.

title: Does the transition to self-employment benefit mental health? Evidence from the UK
authors: Liming Li; Karen Glaser; Ben Geiger
affiliations: Department of Global Health & Social Medicine, King’s College London, UK
abstract: There is limited research evidence on the mental health consequences of self-employment transitions from wage employment. This study fills this gap by investigating this issue using a difference-in-differences design with matching methods employing data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study (2009–2021). The results suggest that transitions to self-employment are associated with a small but significant decrease in psychological distress, signalling improvements in mental health. These effects are stronger among workers with poorer initial mental health when compared to their non-self-employed counterparts. Along with the self-employment transitions, workers also experience declines in socio-economic status but improvements in job autonomy, job satisfaction and satisfaction with leisure time. Overall, these findings highlight the potential protective effects of self-employment on workers’ mental health; however, caution is needed in considering the mental health premium of self-employment transitions.

The Ubiquity of Business Groups around the World: A Property‐Rights Theory
authors: Ruth V. Aguilera; Rafel Crespi‐Cladera; Alfredo Martín‐Oliver; Bartolomé Pascual‐Fuster
affiliations: Northeastern University; Universitat de les Illes Balears
abstract: Abstract Business groups (BGs) are collections of legally independent firms connected by ownership ties and are widely present in both developing and developed economies. We develop property‐rights theory (PRT) to explain this prevalence, extending its scope from the allocation of rights over a bundle of assets to the legal partitioning of assets as another allocative mechanism of property rights. Our conceptual framework complements traditional theories understanding BGs primarily as responses to institutional voids. Drawing on a large global dataset of firms, we examine how firm asset specificity and ownership sharing influence the controlling owners' decision to organize their economic activities as a BG or as a standalone firm. We find that the likelihood of adopting a BG organizational form over a standalone entity increases when (1) controlling owners rely on more firm‐specific assets, and (2) ownership is shared or potentially shared. Moreover, our findings are robust across three commonly observed firm strategic configurations: focused, vertically integrated, and diversified. Our study expands the PRT by developing a theory of property‐rights architecture, moving forward from the institutional voids perspective to explain BGs as efficient governance responses to asset and ownership complexities, hence contributing also to the strategic management and international business literatures.

title: Co‐Constructing the Illusion of Progression: How Boundary Blurring and Affirming Reproduce Social Exclusion in Elite Professions
authors: Stefanie Gustafsson; Laura Empson
affiliations: University of Bath; City University London; Copenhagen Business School
abstract: Abstract Social exclusion is a persistent problem in elite professions. While scholarship has emphasized structural and cultural barriers, less is known about the relational practices and mechanisms through which social exclusion is sustained. Drawing on interviews with 84 lawyers, paralegals, and managers in elite UK law firms, we develop a conceptual model of how the blurring and affirming of social and symbolic boundaries between higher‐status and lower‐status groups reproduces social exclusion. We show how both groups blur and affirm boundaries across three domains: professional work, professional space, and systems of professional advancement. Boundary blurring makes symbolic boundaries more permeable, positioning lower‐status actors as prospective professionals, while boundary affirming maintains social boundaries around professional membership. We identify and theorize the illusion of progression as a relational mechanism emerging from intertwined blurring and affirming, constructing lower‐status roles as pathways into the profession even though progression is rare. The illusion perpetuates liminality by sustaining hope, individualizing failure and undermining lower‐status groups' collective challenge to social exclusion. Our findings advance understanding of the relational mechanism through which social exclusion persists in elite professions, show how boundary blurring can sustain rather than threaten status distinctions, and help explain why organizational diversity and inclusion efforts have produced little substantive change.

title: ON THE CCE ESTIMATION OF THREE-DIMENSIONAL PANELS WITH MULTI-LEVEL FACTORS
authors: Sainan Jin; Xun Lu; Liangjun Su
affiliations: Tsinghua University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong
abstract: Abstract We consider the common correlated effects estimation of a three-dimensional panel data model with heterogeneous slope coefficients and multi-level interactive fixed effects. We study the asymptotic properties of the heterogeneous slope coefficient estimators and the mean group (MG) estimators. We find that bias correction is indispensable for the MG estimator and show that the MG estimators exhibit different convergence rates depending on the degree of heterogeneity in the slope coefficients. We propose a bias correction procedure and inference method that is uniformly valid irrespective of the degree of slope heterogeneity. We conduct Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate the performance of our estimators and inference methods in finite samples. We apply our new methods to international trade data and find significant heterogeneity in the gravity model even after we control for the multi-level factors.

title: Distribution of Researcher-Level Funding Allocation from US Federal Agencies
authors: Deanna Zarrillo; Erjia Yan; Yongjun Zhu; Chaoqun Ni
affiliations: Drexel University College of Computing and Informatics, 3675 Market Street, Philadelphia, PA 19104 (U.S.A.); Yonsei University, Department of Library and Information Science, Seoul, Republic of South Korea; Information School, University of Wisconsin, Madison (U.S.A.)
abstract: Abstract This study examines micro-level trends in research funding by analyzing 12 years of grant distribution data across three major U.S. federal funding agency groups: Department of Health and Human Services, National Science Foundation, and an aggregated group of other agencies. Using longitudinal data on principal investigator funding patterns, grant counts, and distribution metrics including Gini coefficients, we investigate whether cumulative advantage dynamics characterize the U.S. research funding system. We find that HHS demonstrates broader access and a democratization approach to funding, NSF pursues a policy-driven strategy based on sustainable growth while actively preventing accumulation, and other federal agencies implement selective but equitable consolidation of individual funding levels within an elite PI pool. Contrary to expectations of growing inequity, this analysis reveals three distinct strategies aimed at countering cumulative advantage while maintaining agency priorities and facilitating scientific growth.

title: Investigating individual writing style as a contributor to gender gaps in science and technology
authors: Kara Kedrick; Ekaterina Levitskaya; Russell J. Funk
affiliations: Institute for Complex Social Dynamics, Carnegie Mellon University; Coleridge Initiative; Carlson School of Management, University of Minnesota
abstract: Abstract Gender gaps in how scientific work is evaluated are well documented, but their sources remain debated. We ask whether an overlooked factor—the linguistic style of the writing itself—is gendered and consequential. Drawing on a framework that distinguishes informational features (which emphasize facts) from involved features (which emphasize relationships), we analyze single-authored abstracts of academic papers and patents across all fields of science and technology. Women’s writing is systematically more involved than men’s—richer in relational, audience-oriented features and higher in the balance of involved to informational language—a difference that holds across scientific fields, in collaborative and single-authored work, and throughout the full text of a large open-access biomedical corpus, not only their abstracts. This stylistic signature also shapes how work is received—papers whose abstracts are more involved are cited more by women and less by men, and the association persists even when papers are compared against their most content-similar alternatives, indicating a gendered signal independent of topic. That a near-costless feature of writing—word choice rather than substance—leaves a systematic, gendered trace on who cites scientific work points to a subtle channel through which evaluation bias may persist, in tension with the universalist ideal that ideas be judged independently of their author.

title: Gendered collaboration networks and their consequences on conflicts between academics
authors: László Lőrincz; Brigitta Németh; Tamás Felföldi
affiliations: Institute of Data Analytics and Information Systems & ANETI Lab, Corvinus Institute for Advanced Studies, Corvinus University of Budapest, H-1093 Budapest, Fövám tér 8, Hungary; ANETI Lab, Institute for Economics, HUN-REN Centre for Economic and Regional Studies, H-1097 Budapest, Tóth Kálmán utca 4, Hungary; Doctoral School of Economics, Business and Informatics, Corvinus University of Budapest, H-1093 Budapest, Fövám tér 8, Hungary; Corvinus University of Budapest, H-1093 Budapest, Fövám tér 8, Hungary
abstract: Abstract As a major site of knowledge production, academia depends heavily on the quality of interactions among coworkers in collaboration. Negative ties, such as conflicts or avoidance between researchers, can impede the progress of research projects, and adversely affect individual career advancement. Our study reveals that these negative relations are not “gender-neutral” in the academic sector; they are experienced substantially more often by women. Using a large survey of early-career researchers in Hungary linked to administrative scientometric records, we model the number of conflict ties as a function of network position, gender, and field-level diversity. Among women, brokerage in co-authorship networks is associated with more conflicts, whereas embeddedness in cohesive collaboration groups is associated with fewer. These associations are not observed for men, whose conflict ties are more strongly related to publication-related success. Women also report fewer conflicts in fields where women are better represented, although evidence that field diversity moderates the brokerage-conflict relationship is limited. The findings show that collaboration-network advantages are not socially neutral in academia: brokerage may provide professional benefits, but it appears to entail higher interpersonal costs for women.

title: Characteristics of Croatian clinical medicine: a 22-year bibliometric study
authors: Romana Jadrijević; Antonija Mijatović; Daniel Garcia-Costa; Francisco Grimaldo; Ana Marušić
affiliations: University of Split School of Medicine, TRIBE Doctoral Program, 21000 Split, Croatia; University Hospital of Split, Department of Research, 21000 Split, Croatia; University of Split School of Medicine, Center for Evidence-based Medicine, 21000 Split, Croatia; University of Valencia, Department of Electronical Engineering, 46100 Burjassot, Spain; University of Valencia, Department of Computer Science, 46100 Burjassot, Spain
abstract: Abstract Bibliometric analyses have been increasingly used for assessing science, as they provide valuable insights into the dynamics of scientific research. Using the affiliations of Croatian hospitals, we retrieved publications records from Scopus covering the 2003-2024 period and conducted a bibliometric performance analysis. The total number of publications did not statistically significantly increase over time (incidence rate ratio [IRR] per year=1.05, p=0.18). In contrast, the proportion of open-access publications increased significantly (odds ratio [OR] per year=1.21, p<0.001). Median citations per publication exhibited a strong increasing monotonic trend over time (Spearman’s ρ=0.78, p<0.001). The 18 journals with the highest number of publications were all published in Croatia and collectively accounted for 38.5 % of all retrieved publications. Among them, a publication from a single Croatian journal, Biochemia Medica, was in the 100 most-cited publications. The 10 most prolific authors by number of publications were predominantly affiliated with institutions located in the capital of Croatia – Zagreb, which accounted for 64.9 % of all affiliations among these authors. This analysis demonstrated the evolution of scientific research of Croatian clinicians, characterized by growth in open access and citations, as well as a strong geographical centralization.

title: The landscape of Indonesian journal publishing: A country-level analysis of journal and publisher characteristics
authors: Eko Didik Widianto; Hadiyanto Hadiyanto; Teddy Mantoro
affiliations: Doctoral Program of Information Systems, Universitas Diponegoro. Imam Bardjo st., Semarang, Central Java 50241, Indonesia; Department of Computer Engineering, Universitas Diponegoro, Prof. Sudarto st., Semarang, Central Java 50275, Indonesia; School of Postgraduate, Universitas Diponegoro. Imam Bardjo st., Semarang, Central Java 50241, Indonesia; School of Computer Science, Nusa Putra University, Sukabumi, West Java 43152, Indonesia
abstract: Abstract Existing studies on the rapid growth of Indonesian journals focus on metrics but lack the in-depth analysis of their publisher characteristics. This study examines Indonesian journal publishers across four databases: Indonesian Digital References (GARUDA), covering most Indonesian journals; Science and Technology Index (SINTA), covering accredited national journals; Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), covering open-access journals; and Scopus, covering reputable international journals. It analyzes Indonesian publishers by type and size, and their journal standing in national journal accreditation (SINTA) and international indexes (DOAJ, Scopus). The findings show that Indonesian higher education institutions (HEIs) contribute significantly as publishers, with many journals in all databases, alongside government agencies, professional organizations, and commercial publishers. They have the most journals performing well in SINTA accreditation grades, DOAJ criteria, and Scopus rankings. However, many Indonesian journals still face challenges in meeting their objectives for national journal accreditation and inclusion in international indexes. Understanding the country-level journal-publishing landscape is crucial for governments and HEIs to implement data-driven policies that support national journal development. It provides a framework for researchers to explore journal publishing in other countries, enabling an examination of performance and impact using appropriate metrics and databases.

title: From science to policy: A multilevel framework for measuring institutional policy engagement through Overton
authors: Daniel Torres-Salinas; Wenceslao Arroyo-Machado; Nicolas Robinson-Garcia; Esteban Romero Frías
affiliations: Department of Information and Communication Sciences, University of Granada, Granada, Spain; INGENIO (CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València), València, Spain; Department of Accountancy and Finance, University of Granada, Granada, Spain
abstract: Abstract This study presents a multilevel framework to assess the policy attention of academic institutions using Overton as a primary data source. We illustrate this framework through a case study of the University of Granada, combining Overton policy mentions, OpenAlex topics, and bibliometric analysis. Results show policy engagement particularly concentrated in health, physical, and social sciences, with mentions from key governmental and intergovernmental organisations. The study quantifies the university’s visibility in policy documents, classifies mentions by scientific domain and issuer type, maps 1,145 research topics to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and identifies seven researchers whose work aligns with Spain’s Urban Agenda. The findings demonstrate the value of Overton for mapping the presence of institutional research in policy documents and tracing science-policy linkages. However, given the well-documented risks of misuse of bibliometric indicators in research evaluation, users of this framework should be aware of key interpretive boundaries: policy mentions should not be equated with policy impact; raw mention counts cannot establish reliable temporal trends given Overton’s continuous expansion; and geographic and linguistic distributions of mentions reflect Overton’s structural indexing biases toward OECD countries rather than real-world policy engagement. With these caveats, the framework offers a scalable model for institutional policy engagement assessment.

title: Great Expectations? Researchers in Germany are Optimistic about the Potential of Grant Lotteries
authors: Christophe Heger
affiliations: Deutsches Zentrum für Hochschul- und Wissenschaftsforschung (DZHW)
abstract: Abstract In this study I investigate researchers’ expectations towards the potential advantages of grant lotteries in a representative sample of scientists at German universities and higher education institutions provided by the Scientists Survey of the German Centre for Higher Education Research and Science Studies (DZHW). I describe the saliency of the two debates on bias in grant peer review and on grant lotteries, as well as researchers’ levels of experience with grant peer review. I use both descriptive statistics and analytical models to investigate which characteristics shape scientists’ relative grant lottery optimism. I find that experienced and more senior scientists are significantly less optimistic about grant lotteries. Saliency and reviewer workload are positively associated with optimism. I conclude that, even though saliency of the issue remains sparse, researchers are generally optimistic about grant lotteries, yet also aware of some of their potential disadvantages.

title: Exploring Cross-Grant Interactions in Research Funding: "Amplifying What Is Possible"
authors: Andreas Kjær Stage; Duncan Andrew Thomas; Irene Ramos-Vielba; Carter Walter Bloch
affiliations: Danish Centre for Studies in Research and Research Policy, Department of Political Science, Aarhus University, Bartholins Allé 8, 8000 Aarhus C, Denmark; Steno Diabetes Center Aarhus, Aarhus University Hospital, Palle Juul-Jensens Boulevard 11, Aarhus N 8200, Denmark; Department for Health, University of Bath, Claverton Down, Bath, United Kingdom; Institute for Advanced Social Studies, Spanish National Research Council (IESA-CSIC), Campo Santo de los Mártires 7, Córdoba, 14004 Spain
abstract: Abstract Researchers often work across multiple concurrent grants, yet studies of research funding, its features, goals, and impacts, typically examine single grants in isolation. This overlooks the broader context of funding configurations within which researchers organize their work. This exploratory paper explores cross-grant interactions (or co-use), through interviews and mapping of the grant configurations of 12 principal investigators in Denmark, the Netherlands, and Norway. The analysis shows that cross-grant interactions were reported in both parallel and sequential forms, enabled mainly by overlaps of people, infrastructure, and knowledge. Interviewees described such interactions as producing beneficial synergies, including expanded capacity and knowledge transfer, while also identifying grey zones related to attribution, administration, funder rules, and personnel or resource allocation. The funding configurations were more heterogeneous than expected in size, grant number, funder origin, researcher role, and funder requirements. This heterogeneity limited the identification of stable configuration archetypes in the present sample. It nevertheless demonstrates that single-grant approaches can miss much of the funding context relevant to research practice and evaluation. The paper calls for greater attention to cross-grant interactions, not by treating all overlap as either misuse or synergy, but to develop practices that make legitimate co-use visible, assessable, and, where appropriate, supportable.

title: Stratification and Integration in the Key Research Specialty of Women in Science and Engineering, Over Time
authors: Mary Frank Fox; Gerhard Sonnert; Emma Menardi; Derek McNutt
affiliations: Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter School of Public Policy Georgia Institute of Technology Atlanta, Georgia 30332, USA; Center for Astrophysics Harvard University Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138, USA; Department of Sociology Princeton University Princeton, New Jersey 08544, USA
abstract: Abstract We examine the features of focal and non-focal groups of authors (measured by thresholds of their publication counts) in the research specialty of women in science and engineering. This specialty is important because of the ways in which it relates to science, gender, and society. The study combines a bibliometric approach with a social-structural perspective. Our research questions focus on the features of the groups of authors–-metrics of levels of stratification and integration-in a consequential 45-year period (1965-2010 for articles, and through 2021 for citations). The study employs a systematic, multi-stage design that finds and verifies 3,174 articles belonging to the specialty out of 23,000 retrieved; and identifies the authors of these articles and their features. The results are contrary to our expectation of this specialty being “exceptional” in relatively low stratification among authors. Findings point to divisions by focal and non-focal groups; substantial inequality in skewed publication productivity, citations, and affiliations; integration among the focal group in co-authorship and clusters; and complexities of stratifiation and integration over time. The study suggests fruitful continuing inquiries and demonstrates the potential of combining a bibliometric approach and social-structural perspectives in understanding authors in this, and other specialties.

title: The strength of weird ties: positive genetic interactions have greater scientific impact but are under-represented in the literature
authors: Mengyi Sun; David M. McCandlish
affiliations: Simons Center for Quantitative Biology, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, Cold Spring Harbor, NY, 11724, USA
abstract: Abstract Genetic interactions, where mutating two genes together affects a trait differently than expected from their individual effects, often reveal how genes work together. When the trait is cell growth, systematic studies show that negative interactions (worse than expected) usually link functionally related genes and are widely considered informative, whereas positive interactions (better than expected) tend to link seemingly unrelated genes and are often deemed less informative. However, the sociology of science suggests that transformative discoveries often arise from unexpected, cross-domain connections. To evaluate these competing perspectives, we linked large-scale yeast interaction data to the literature on each gene pair and its citations. Contrary to prevailing assumptions, papers on positively interacting gene pairs tend to be more highly cited. Yet positive interactions are significantly under-represented in the literature relative to their experimental prevalence. This gap persisted after a technology detecting both types equally well became available, implicating factors beyond mere discoverability. Research building on positive interactions also forms a more interconnected body of work. These findings reveal the underappreciated value of positive interactions. More broadly, they show how science-of-science insights can identify biases in biomedical research and provide concrete guidance on what to study next.

title: Open Editors Plus: A Comprehensive Dataset of Editorial Board Composition Across 15,000 Academic Journals
authors: Basile Chretien
affiliations: Neuropresage Team (PhIND, UMR-S U1237), Normandie Université, UNICAEN, INSERM, GIP Cyceron, Caen, France
abstract: Abstract Editorial boards serve as central gatekeepers in scholarly publishing, yet comprehensive, enriched data on their composition has remained scarce. We introduce Open Editors Plus, a dataset of 922,097 editorial board positions across 15,168 journals from 48 publishers, covering 745,125 unique editors in 189 countries. Each record is enriched with algorithmically inferred gender, institutional geolocation via the Research Organization Registry, bibliometric indicators from OpenAlex, and journal indexing status across five major databases. Among editors with gender-resolvable names (primarily European-origin; 18% of records are unresolved; 82% resolved), 33% are women, with Editors-in-Chief at 24.9%. Geographic concentration is extreme (Gini = 0.90); the top 10 countries hold 71% of positions. One in four editors serves on multiple boards, and multi-board editors have substantially higher h-indices. The dataset is released under CC0 on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21620278) with an interactive explorer at openeditors-plus.org.

title: Are the Hedges of Funds Green?
authors: Huan Kuang; Bing Liang; Mila Getmansky Sherman; Tianyi Qu
affiliations: Bryant University College of Business; University of Massachusetts Amherst Isenberg School of Management Finance; Baylor University Finance Department
abstract: Abstract Over the past decade, hedge funds have increasingly embraced green investing. We develop a novel return-based measure of fund greenness and find that greener funds earn higher average returns, consistent with capturing a positive green premium, and are associated with lower risks, especially during adverse periods. We further show that performance gains are greatest among directional funds, whereas risk reduction is most pronounced among nondirectional funds. We also provide evidence that managers of these funds exhibit superior green investment skills through green stock selection and green factor timing. Finally, investors reward greener hedge funds only when they demonstrate strong performance.

title: Large Funds and Corporate Bond Market Fragility
authors: Yong Chen; Mengqiao Du; Zheng Sun
affiliations: Texas A&M University; National University of; University of California , Irvine
abstract: Abstract The corporate bond fund industry is characterized by a high concentration of capital, with a substantial portion of assets managed by large funds. We examine the relation between large-fund trading exposure and corporate bond volatility across market conditions. Using a comprehensive sample of U.S. bond funds and corporate bonds, we show that bond return volatility decreases (increases) with trading fund size when market liquidity is high (low). Exploring the underlying mechanisms, we find that large funds are more likely to reach for yield by holding illiquid bonds. Further analysis suggests that while large funds supply liquidity during normal times, their liquidity-supplying activity weakens during market stress. Finally, large funds tend to sell illiquid bonds when facing investor outflows during illiquid markets. Overall, our findings reveal an important yet subtle relation between fund size and bond market fragility, akin to a “dam effect.” JEL Classification: G10, G12, G23

title: Fisher Dynamics, Monetary Policy, and Household Indebtedness
authors: ANDREAS FAGERENG; MAGNUS A. H. GULBRANDSEN; MARTIN B. HOLM; GISLE J. NATVIK
abstract: Abstract Growth in household debt‐to‐income ratios reflects nominal debt changes or “Fisher dynamics” due to interest income and expenses, real income growth, and inflation. Using two decades of microdata on all Norwegian households, we decompose these channels' roles in how debt‐to‐income evolves over time and in response to monetary policy shocks. On average, debt changes outsize Fisher dynamics, except among highly leveraged households. After interest rate hikes, the channels pull in opposite directions, but the debt changes dominate, so debt‐to‐income ratios decline. This holds across subgroups, including highly indebted households, recent movers, and those facing liquidity constraints or high unemployment risk.

title: Board–CEO Trust and Concealing Adverse News
authors: Kee-Hong Bae; Sadok El Ghoul; Zhaoran Gong; Omrane Guedhami; Lixin Su
affiliations: York University; The University of Texas at El Paso; University of South Carolina
abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate how generalized trust, a culturally rooted belief in the trustworthiness of unfamiliar others, influences board oversight. Using an ancestry-based measure of board–CEO trust based on ancestral origins and bilateral trust scores across countries, we find a significant positive relation between board–CEO trust and stock price crash risk, indicating higher bad-news hoarding. This relation remains robust across alternative crash risk measures, sample specifications, and trust measures. Firms with high board–CEO trust exhibit more asymmetric stock market reactions to good news versus bad news and a higher likelihood of material restatements. Analyses of insider trading patterns show that directors in high-trust firms are less informed than CEOs about adverse developments, supporting lax board monitoring rather than collusion between directors and CEOs. Overall, the evidence suggests that culturally inherited trust can weaken board oversight and reduce corporate transparency, consistent with an underexplored governance friction even within well-structured boards. title: The Anti‐SLAPP Statutes and Corporate Environmental Policies
authors: KEVIN C.W. CHEN; ZHIHONG CHEN; CHENGZHU SUN
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; Hong Kong Polytechnic University
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether legal protection for civic participation affects corporate pollution. Polluters may deter public discipline through strategic lawsuits. Anti‐SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) statutes mitigate this threat by enabling prompt dismissal and recovery of legal costs. Using a difference‐in‐differences design, we find that enacting an anti‐SLAPP statute in a state significantly reduces toxic emissions from that state by increasing local public pressure. The reduction is greater when the statutes provide stronger protection, when local stakeholders have stronger incentives and abilities to discipline polluters, and when local public pressure increases more after the enactment. Plants lower emissions by improving abatement rather than by reducing output or relocating emissions. Our paper underscores the role of legal protection in environmental governance and informs policy debates over anti‐SLAPP legislation.

title:
Using Financial Accounting Information to Estimate the Income Shifting of
                    <scp>US</scp>
                    Multinationals
authors: Scott D. Dyreng; Robert Hills; Kevin S. Markle
affiliations: Duke University Durham North Carolina USA; University of Georgia Athens Georgia USA; Michigan State University East Lansing Michigan USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Existing estimates of how much income US multinational corporations (MNCs) shift out of the United States differ dramatically, and most cannot identify which specific firms do the shifting. We use data from firms' public financial reports to derive firm‐year estimates of US MNCs' outbound income shifting. We find that aggregate US outbound income shifting is substantially lower than widely cited macroeconomic‐based estimates, with the gap driven primarily by double counting of foreign income in macroeconomic data rather than by differences in firms' sensitivity to tax rates. Income shifting is also highly concentrated among a small number of firms, primarily in intangible‐intensive industries such as computers and pharmaceuticals, while most MNCs shift little or no income. This concentration implies that size‐based thresholds embedded in the OECD's Pillar 2 and the US corporate alternative minimum tax will capture the most active income shifters but may also impose compliance burdens on many firms that shift minimal income. These findings have direct implications for policy‐makers designing international tax rules, tax authorities prioritizing audit resources toward high‐risk income shifters, and investors and lenders assessing MNCs' tax‐related exposures.

title: The Seeds of State Capture: Merit and Patrimonialism in the Colonial Bureaucracy
authors: SARAH BRIERLEY; NOAH NATHAN; GEORGE KWAKU OFOSU; TINGXUAN ZHU
affiliations: London School of Economics and Political Science; Massachusetts Institute of Technology
abstract: Bureaucracies vary in the extent to which hiring is meritocratic versus patrimonial. Such outcomes are typically seen as the result of politicians’ behavior. However, politicians often delegate hiring to existing bureaucrats. When political leaders are socially distant from communities they seek to govern and these areas are peripheral to politicians’ core interests, bureaucrats’ private preferences can dominate hiring decisions instead. Colonial and other forms of external state-building typify cases where patrimonialism created by bureaucrats, not politicians, can emerge. Digitizing individual-level records across six decades of British rule in Ghana, we find evidence of patrimonialism rather than meritocracy in the hiring of African staff, with large inequities across ethnic groups. Our results demonstrate the underexplored agency of local bureaucrats in state-building and highlight conditions under which bureaucrats’ preferences, rather than only political principals’, shape state institutions. They also challenge conventional wisdom about why, and when, newly-independent African states became “neopatrimonial.”

title: The Influence of Police Unions in Local Elections: Evidence from U.S. Cities’ Spending and Performance
authors: MARIA CARRERI; EDOARDO TESO; RUI YU
affiliations: Bocconi University; Amazon
abstract: Despite growing attention to local policies governing public safety issues, and mounting reports of police union spending to local candidates, the role of police unions in local politics remains understudied. We address this gap by assembling a novel, large-scale dataset on campaign finance in U.S. mayoral elections, covering 2,303 races across 1,073 cities from 2001 to 2019. We document that police unions frequently donate to mayoral candidates—especially in mid-sized and large cities—targeting likely winners and incumbents, and without displaying clear partisan bias. Using a within-city design that accounts for heterogeneous treatment effects in the presence of staggered treatment timing, we find that the election of a police-union-backed mayor leads to an expansion in police department size. However, we do not find improvements in police performance in these cities, suggesting that unions’ political involvement, while providing additional resources, might also be associated with reduced incentives for effort.

title: Who’s Asking Whom? Gendering in Parliamentary Interactions
authors: Denisa Kostovicova; Tolga Sinmazdemir; Lanabi La Lova; Vesna Popovski
affiliations: The London School of Economics and Political Science; SOAS University of London
abstract: Abstract Male domination is asserted and reproduced through speaking behavior in parliaments. We address the enduring challenge of women’s marginalization by examining the interactive nature of speech. People adjust their speaking behavior based on the gender and status of those with whom they interact. Analyzing over 2,500 question-and-answer sequences in the Croatian Parliament (2004–20), we identify interactional asymmetry: male MPs ask fewer and shorter questions of female ministers than of male ministers, and engage in shorter exchanges with women than with men. Notably, female MPs partially replicate this pattern, posing shorter questions to female ministers. Female ministers, however, use their executive status to assert authority and respond with longer answers than men, despite their marginalization as women. We reveal how non-cooperation through withholding speech and limiting engagement with women operates as a form of power in interactions, reproducing parliaments as masculine institutions whilst affecting the quality of government oversight.
